advisory.title: Possible arbitrary file write and read in Active Storage image analysis
advisory.description:
### Impact

A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an
unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when
attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable
by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base`
and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to
remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details

ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some
coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself.
Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick
analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted
file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no
variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One specific attack chain has
been reported to us, but we do not assume it is the only one that exists.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy and prepend its
directory to `MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH` through `MiniMagick.cli_env`, so every
ImageMagick process that MiniMagick spawns applies it. The policy denies the
`MSL` scripting coder, the coders that read or delete files other than the
image, fetch remote or local references, or display to a screen, every coder
backed by Ghostscript together with the `gs` delegate, and `@filename`
indirection. ImageMagick applies every `policy.xml` on its search path, so the
shipped policy adds to the host's policy rather than replacing it. The policy
applies to every ImageMagick command that MiniMagick runs, not only those of
Active Storage. See the `activestorage` CHANGELOG and "ImageMagick Security
Policy" in the Active Storage guide.

### Affected applications

An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. This is
  `config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick`, which is the
  default for applications on `load_defaults 6.1` or earlier.
- Runs ImageMagick under a security policy that does not already deny the
  coders involved. The policies that Debian and Ubuntu package do not.
- Allows file uploads from untrusted users.

### Mitigation

- Upgrade to a fixed version of `activestorage`.
- An application whose variant processor is `:mini_magick` must use
  mini_magick `>= 5.1`, which applying the policy requires. With an older
  mini_magick, such an application raises an exception during boot.
- An application that renders PostScript or PDF through ImageMagick must
  re-allow the `gs` delegate and the coders it uses in the host's
  `policy.xml`.
- An application that replaces `MiniMagick.cli_env` after boot, clears the
  environment with `MiniMagick.cli_prefix`, or installs its own
  `MiniMagick::Shell` does not receive the shipped policy and must carry its
  rules in ImageMagick's system policy. GraphicsMagick does not read
  ImageMagick policies.
- If attachments are stored with the Disk service, change `secret_key_base`
  and every secret readable by the application process, including the master
  key and everything `config/credentials.yml.enc` holds, storage and database
  credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not retain an exposed secret as a
  fallback.

### Workarounds

Copy the rules of the policy that the fixed versions ship,
`activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml`, into ImageMagick's
system policy, for example `/etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml`. At a minimum, deny
the `MSL` coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the `gs` delegate:

```xml
<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="MSL"/>
<policy domain="delegate" rights="none" pattern="gs"/>
<policy domain="coder" rights="none" pattern="{PS,PS2,PS3,EPS,EPS2,EPS3,EPI,EPSF,EPSI,EPT,EPT2,EPT3,PDF,AI,EPDF,PDFA,POCKETMOD,XPS,PCL}"/>
```

### Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/468aa9a93fc98f5476b6821770f4ccfcb7f7d328
- 8.0:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/ea8c40121ce53a3d0255cd4eb6d13bfe3bc01776

### Versions affected

- activestorage < 8.0.5.2
- activestorage >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher
[ryotak](https://hackerone.com/ryotak).

### References

- ImageMagick [security policy](https://imagemagick.org/security-policy/)

advisory.title: Possible circumvention of file size limits in Active Storage direct uploads to Google Cloud Storage
advisory.description:
### Impact

`ActiveStorage::Service::GCSService#url_for_direct_upload` does not bind the
declared content length into the signed direct-upload URL, and
`#headers_for_direct_upload` returns no length constraint, so the URL
authorizes an upload body of any size. A direct-upload client could store a
file larger than the `byte_size` it declared, and the resulting blob keeps the
declared size, possibly bypassing application file size validations and
quotas. This is the weakness that CVE-2020-8162 fixed in the S3 service.

Applications that store files in Google Cloud Storage and accept direct
uploads are affected.

### Details

The fixed releases sign an `x-goog-content-length-range` header that matches
the blob's declared `byte_size` and return it from
`headers_for_direct_upload`, so Cloud Storage rejects an upload body of any
other size. Browsers send this header with the direct upload, so a bucket's
CORS configuration must list `x-goog-content-length-range` in
`responseHeader`, or browser direct uploads fail after the upgrade. The Active
Storage CHANGELOG and the CORS example in the Active Storage guide show the
change.

### Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/e19916cea31cbfb0030b165ae853b741f8dd57a7.patch
- 8.0:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/7fe85a72a789eae5ee070ce3ee1dad10a8a5f70c.patch

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher
[f4cts](https://hackerone.com/f4cts).

advisory.title: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Storage filename handling
advisory.description:
### Impact

`ActiveStorage::Filename#base` and `#extension_with_delimiter`, and therefore
`#extension`, pass the stored filename unmodified to `File.basename` and
`File.extname`, which raise `ArgumentError` when the name contains a NUL byte.
Active Storage stores the client-supplied filename verbatim, so a user who is
permitted to upload an attachment could persist such a filename on databases
that accept NUL bytes in string columns, such as SQLite and MySQL/MariaDB.
Each subsequent request that builds a variant or preview of the blob, opens
it, or renders it as an Action Text attachment then raises, possibly resulting
in a persistent DoS vulnerability for the pages that display the blob until it
is purged or its filename is corrected. Applications that use PostgreSQL are
not affected, because PostgreSQL rejects the row.

### Details

`Filename#base` and `#extension_with_delimiter` now derive from
`Filename#sanitized`, the form that `Filename#to_s` and the
`Content-Disposition` header already use. For a filename that `#sanitized`
changes, such as one containing a NUL byte, an invalid byte sequence, a path
separator or another replaced character, the base and extension now agree with
`#to_s`; the variant format inferred from such a name may change, and an
existing variant may be regenerated once. Stored filenames are not modified,
and no data migration is required.

### Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/60f22af88b71eae251f112d8c0237a08a8832692.patch
- 8.0:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/9b0d4bef2211a2c08cab2e0ea17fa1d0efd5d47a.patch

### Credit

This issue was found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner (ANT-2026-UQM5Z4YL).

advisory.title: Possible arbitrary file read and remote code execution in Active Storage video previews, analysis and image processing
advisory.description:
### Impact

`ActiveStorage::Blob#open` writes a blob to a tempfile whose name carries the
extension of the uploaded filename, and hands that path to `ffprobe`
(`VideoAnalyzer`, `AudioAnalyzer`), `ffmpeg` (`VideoPreviewer`) and
ImageMagick (`ImageAnalyzer`, the `:mini_magick` variant processor). These
tools select a decoder from the file extension when the content does not
identify its own format, so an attacker who chooses the filename and declares
the content type of an upload chooses which decoder processes it. An FFmpeg
built with AviSynth support treats a file with the `.avs` extension as an
AviSynth script and evaluates it, which could disclose files readable by the
application process through the preview image, or load a native library the
attacker has also uploaded, possibly leading to remote code execution in the
FFmpeg process. ImageMagick selects its coders and delegates from the
extension in the same way.

### Details

The fixed releases keep the uploaded extension on the tempfile only when
Marcel maps that extension to the blob's recorded content type, and name the
tempfile with no extension otherwise. A form upload whose Rack tempfile fails
the same check is copied to a correctly named tempfile before processing.
Files whose uploaded extension disagrees with their content type are still
processed; the external tool detects their format from the content. The Active
Storage CHANGELOG describes the change.

### Affected applications

An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Accepts uploads from untrusted users.
- Analyzes video or audio attachments (which Active Storage does on attach by
  default), generates video previews, or processes images with ImageMagick.

The AviSynth attack additionally requires an FFmpeg built with
`--enable-avisynth` and the AviSynthPlus runtime on the host. Upstream FFmpeg
and the common Linux distribution and Homebrew packages do not enable it; the
GPL builds distributed for Windows and Linux from ffmpeg.org do. Other
decoders that FFmpeg or ImageMagick select from the extension may be reachable
without AviSynth.

### Mitigation

- Upgrade to a fixed version of `activestorage`.

### Expire and change secrets

Upgrading closes the vulnerability but does not undo a disclosure that already
occurred. An application that meets the AviSynth requirement above should
treat every secret readable by the application process as potentially exposed
and change it, including `secret_key_base`, the master key and everything in
`config/credentials.yml.enc` that it decrypts, the Active Storage service
credentials, database credentials, and tokens for third-party services.
Changing `secret_key_base` expires active sessions and invalidates signed and
encrypted cookies, signed global IDs and Active Storage URLs. Do not retain an
exposed secret as a fallback.

### Workarounds

Applications that cannot upgrade can stop Active Storage from running FFmpeg
on uploaded files by removing `ActiveStorage::Previewer::VideoPreviewer` from
`config.active_storage.previewers`, and
`ActiveStorage::Analyzer::VideoAnalyzer` and
`ActiveStorage::Analyzer::AudioAnalyzer` from
`config.active_storage.analyzers`. Running an FFmpeg built without AviSynth
support closes the AviSynth attack but not the extension-selected decoders of
ImageMagick.

### Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/72136ff39153bc8d63ecbc899993848eb3d6573e.patch
- 8.0:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/8106938fb0a595f11006dd1497cd409e27d7d636.patch

### Versions affected

- activestorage < 8.0.5.2
- activestorage >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by HackerOne researcher
[pirikara](https://hackerone.com/pirikara).

advisory.title: Rails Active Support has a possible ReDoS vulnerability in number_to_delimited
advisory.description:
### Impact
`NumberToDelimitedConverter` used a regular expression with `gsub!` to insert thousands delimiters.
This could produce quadratic time complexity on long digit strings.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

advisory.title: Rails Active Support has a possible XSS vulnerability in SafeBuffer#%
advisory.description:
### Impact
`SafeBuffer#%` does not propagate the `@html_unsafe` flag to the newly created buffer.
If a `SafeBuffer` is mutated in place (e.g. via `gsub!`) and then formatted with `%` using untrusted arguments,
the result incorrectly reports `html_safe? == true`, bypassing ERB auto-escaping and possibly leading to XSS.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

advisory.title: Rails Active Support has a possible DoS vulnerability in its number helpers
advisory.description:
### Impact
Active Support number helpers accept strings containing scientific notation (e.g. `1e10000`),
which when converted to a string could be expanded into extremely large decimal representations.
This can cause excessive memory allocation and CPU consumption when the expanded number is formatted,
possibly resulting in a DoS vulnerability.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

advisory.title: Possible DoS vulnerability in Active Support safe_constantize
advisory.description:
### Impact

When constant lookup raises `LoadError`,
`ActiveSupport::Inflector#safe_constantize` (and `String#safe_constantize`)
builds a regular expression from the requested constant name without escaping
it, so a caller that passes untrusted input lets the attacker choose the
source of a pattern that the application compiles. Crafted patterns can
trigger defects in Ruby's regular expression compiler, possibly leading to a
crash of the server process, and repeated requests could keep the application
unavailable.

Action Cable passes the `channel` value of each `subscribe` command to
`safe_constantize` before any channel lookup, so in the default configuration
an unauthenticated client of the Action Cable endpoint can reach this code.

### Details

The check that decides whether `safe_constantize` returns `nil` or re-raises
the `LoadError` now matches the first segment of the constant name against the
error message as a literal string, and no longer compiles a regular
expression. It returns the same result as before for constant names that
contain no regular expression syntax.

### Affected applications

An application is affected if it meets all of these requirements:
- Mounts Action Cable, which a new Rails application does by default at
  `/cable` (`config.action_cable.mount_path`), or otherwise passes untrusted
  input to `safe_constantize`.
- Accepts Action Cable connections from untrusted clients.
  `ApplicationCable::Connection#connect` authenticates nobody unless the
  application adds a check.

### Workarounds

Applications that do not use Action Cable can set
`config.action_cable.mount_path = nil` to remove the endpoint. Applications
that use Action Cable can call `reject_unauthorized_connection` in
`ApplicationCable::Connection#connect` for unauthenticated clients, which
limits exposure to authenticated users but does not remove it.

### Releases

The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/95aa9e416016524956d4904fed96eaed079580bb.patch
- 8.0:
  https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/210ac22d446c8e2625b091e79256806b836eee20.patch

### Versions affected

- activesupport < 8.0.5.2
- activesupport >= 8.1, < 8.1.4.1

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Felix Tscheulin
([flixt](https://hackerone.com/flixt)) through HackerOne researcher
[scheja](https://hackerone.com/scheja), and independently by Bucky Wolfe
([Igneous](https://github.com/Igneous)), who provided a proof of concept that
crashes the server. It was also found by the Anthropic OSS Scanner
(ANT-2026-ZUN5KU3Q).

advisory.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service in Addressable templates with several exploded variables
advisory.description:
Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, expressions
with several exploded variables (e.g., {+a*,b*}, {+a*,b*,c*},
{/a*,b*}, {?a*,b*}) generate regular expressions vulnerable to
excessive backtracking. A run of members can be divided among the
exploded variables in O(n^k) ways for k variables. When Template#match
or Template#extract is called with a maliciously crafted URI, this
can result in uncontrolled resource consumption, leading to denial
of service. With 2.9.0, {+a*,b*,c*} takes over 12 seconds to reject
1 KB of input on MRI Ruby 3.2.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the
URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only
call Template#expand are unaffected.

## Credits

Reported by Daniel Coles (@manus-pi).

advisory.title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts containing bidi and invisible characters
advisory.description:
Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning
with xn--) that contain characters which change how text is displayed
without being visible themselves. These include bidirectional controls
such as U+202E RIGHT-TO-LEFT OVERRIDE and U+2066–U+2069, zero-width
characters, and other invisible format characters.
Addressable::URI#display_uri uses to_unicode, so it can display a
host whose characters appear reordered or which looks identical to
a different host. For example, the host of http://xn--abcmoc-dm0c.com/
is displayed as abc, U+202E, moc.com, and the override makes
everything after abc render right to left.

Parsing, host, normalized_host and any connection made from the URI
are not affected. Only the displayed form is. Applications that
show display_uri to users (link previews, chat and email clients,
admin interfaces) can be used to make a malicious domain look
like a trusted one.

In the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation, all such characters are
decoded, including those that IDNA's nameprep profile prohibits.
In the native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the idn-ruby
gem are installed, libidn rejects most of them, but not characters
added to Unicode after version 3.2, such as U+061C and U+2066–U+2069.

## Credits

Reported by @andrewstellman.

advisory.title: Addressable URI normalization resolves some dotted path segments to the wrong path
advisory.description:
Addressable::URI.normalize_path resolves some paths containing ..
segments to a different path than RFC 3986 does. When a path climbs
above the root before any other .. is resolved, the segments that
later .. segments should remove are instead kept:
/../../public/x/../../secret normalizes to /public/x/secret instead
of /secret. URI#normalize, URI#join, URI#== and URI#=== all use
this normalization. An application that checks a normalized Addressable
path against an allowlist, but sends the original URI to something
that resolves it according to RFC 3986, can be made to allow a
request for a path outside the allowlist.

advisory.title: Addressable display_uri can show misleading hosts with invalid Punycode A-labels
advisory.description:
Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode, in the pure-Ruby IDNA implementation,
decodes Punycode labels (labels beginning with xn--) that are not
valid A-labels. Those labels are returned in decoded form, when
they should be returned unchanged. That includes:

* labels that decode to only ASCII characters, e.g. xn--google-
  decodes to google;
* labels that decode to text that doesn't convert back to the same
  label (RFC 3490 §4.2), e.g. text that isn't in normalized form.

Addressable::URI#display_uri uses to_unicode, so for
https://xn--google-.example.org/ it displays the host google.example.org,
while #host, #normalized_host and any connection made from the URI
use xn--google-.example.org. An attacker who controls a domain can
therefore have a URI displayed as a host they don't control.
Applications that compare the result of to_unicode against a list
of trusted names can likewise treat two different hosts as the same.

The native IDNA implementation, used when libidn and the idn-ruby
gem are installed, is not affected. to_ascii and normalized_host
are not affected.

## Credits

Reported by @tonghuaroot.

advisory.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service in Addressable templates with multiple variables
advisory.description:
Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates
that put several variables in one expression generate regular
expressions vulnerable to excessive backtracking:

1. Expressions with any operator other than + and # (e.g., {/owner,repo,ref},
   {.a,b}, {a,b,c}, {;a,b,c}). The values are joined by an optional
   separator, so a run of characters can be divided among the variables
   in O(n^k) ways for k variables.
2. Expressions with the + or # operators and many variables (e.g.,
   {+v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6,v7,v8,v9,v10}). A failing match is exponential
   in the number of variables.
3. Several single-variable expressions next to each other (e.g.,
   {+a}{+b}{+c} or {a}{b}{c}), which are polynomial in the input length.

When Template#match or Template#extract is called with a maliciously
crafted URI, this can result in uncontrolled resource consumption,
leading to denial of service. A three-variable path template such
as http://example.com/repos{/owner,repo,ref} needs about 2 KB of
input to occupy a thread for many seconds.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the
URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who only
call Template#expand are unaffected.

## Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem Security.

advisory.title: Regular Expression Denial of Service in Addressable templates with certain exploded expressions
advisory.description:
Within the URI template implementation in Addressable, templates
using the * (explode) modifier with the /, ., ;, ? or & operators
(e.g., {/segments*}, {.ext*}, {;params*}, {?query*}) generate
regular expressions vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking. When
Template#match or Template#extract is called with a maliciously
crafted URI that starts with the operator's leading character,
matching takes exponential time, leading to uncontrolled resource
consumption and denial of service. An input under 60 bytes is
enough to occupy a thread for minutes.

GHSA-h27x-rffw-24p4 (CVE-2026-35611) reported this pattern as
fully remediated in 2.9.0. The 2.9.0 fix only made the joiner
between exploded members mandatory for templates without an operator,
and its regression specs used inputs that never start with the
operator's leading character, so the vulnerable part of the
expression was never reached. This issue was originally reported
in #364 by @ebenoist in 2019 but insufficiently investigated.

Users of the URI parsing capabilities in Addressable but not the
URI template matching capabilities are unaffected. Users who
only call Template#expand are unaffected.

## Credits

Reported independently by @ebenoist, @andrewstellman, and
then @halogenandtoast.

advisory.title: Denial of service in Addressable URI path normalization
advisory.description:
Addressable::URI.normalize_path takes time quadratic in the number
of nested dot segments in a path (e.g., "/" + "a/" * n + "../" * n,
which for n = 3 is /a/a/a/../../../), because it removes one dot
segment per pass over the whole path. URI#normalize, URI#normalized_path,
URI#==, URI#=== and URI#join all call it. Normalizing, comparing or
joining a URI taken from user input can result in uncontrolled
resource consumption, leading to denial of service. On 2.9.0,
normalizing a 34 KB path takes about 3.5 seconds on MRI Ruby 4.0,
and the cost grows with the square of the path length.

This affects every Ruby implementation, including MRI Ruby 3.2 and
later. URI.parse by itself is unaffected, as is code that never
normalizes, compares, or joins URIs from untrusted sources.

## Credits

Reported by Matthew Mongeau (@halogenandtoast), Ruby Central Gem
Security, who also suggested the single-pass approach used in the fix.

advisory.title: Concurrent Ruby - `AtomicReference#update` livelocks when the stored value is `Float::NAN`
advisory.description:
### Summary

`Concurrent::AtomicReference#update` can enter a permanent busy retry
loop when the current value is `Float::NAN`.

The issue is caused by the interaction between:
- `AtomicReference#update`, which retries until `compare_and_set(old_value,
  new_value)` succeeds.
- Numeric `compare_and_set`, which checks `old == old_value` before
  attempting the underlying atomic swap.
- Ruby NaN semantics, where `Float::NAN == Float::NAN` is always `false`.

As a result, once an `AtomicReference` contains `Float::NAN`, calling
`#update` repeatedly evaluates the caller's block and never returns.
In services that store externally derived numeric values in an
`AtomicReference`, this can cause CPU exhaustion or permanent
request/job hangs.

### Impact

This is an application-level denial of service issue. If an application
stores externally derived numeric data in a `Concurrent::AtomicReference`,
an attacker or faulty upstream data source may be able to cause the
stored value to become `Float::NAN`. Any later call to
`AtomicReference#update` on that reference will spin indefinitely,
repeatedly executing the update block and consuming CPU.

### Credit

Pranjali Thakur - depthfirst ([depthfirst.com](<http://depthfirst.com>))

advisory.title: Concurrent Ruby - `ReentrantReadWriteLock` read-count overflow grants a write lock without exclusivity
advisory.description:
### Summary

`Concurrent::ReentrantReadWriteLock` can incorrectly grant a write lock
after one thread acquires the read lock 32,768 times.

The lock stores a thread's local read and write hold counts in one
integer. The low 15 bits are used for the read hold count, and bit 15
is used as `WRITE_LOCK_HELD`. After 32,768 reentrant read acquisitions,
the local read count crosses into the write-lock bit. `try_write_lock`
then treats the thread as already holding a write lock and returns
`true` without setting the global `RUNNING_WRITER` bit.

This breaks the core mutual-exclusion guarantee: the caller is told
it has a write lock, but other threads can still hold or acquire
read locks at the same time.

### Impact

This breaks the write-lock exclusivity guarantee. After the overflow,
a thread can be told it has acquired the write lock while other threads
can still hold or acquire read locks, allowing races and inconsistent
reads of protected mutable state.

### Credit

Pranjali Thakur - depthfirst ([depthfirst.com](<http://depthfirst.com>))

advisory.title: Concurrent Ruby - ReadWriteLock allows wrong-thread write release and stray read-release counter corruption
advisory.description:
### Summary

`Concurrent::ReadWriteLock#release_write_lock` does not verify that the
calling thread acquired the write lock. Any thread with access to the
lock object can release an active write lock held by another thread. A
second writer can then enter its critical section while the first writer
is still running.

`Concurrent::ReadWriteLock#release_read_lock` also decrements the shared
counter even when no read lock is held. Calling it on a fresh lock
changes the counter from `0` to `-1`, after which normal read acquisition
raises `Concurrent::ResourceLimitError`.

This is a synchronization correctness issue in the public
`Concurrent::ReadWriteLock` API. It should not be framed as an
authorization bypass; the lock is an in-process concurrency primitive,
not an access-control boundary.

### Impact

This can break the write-lock mutual exclusion guarantee and can also
leave a lock unusable after a stray read release.
The impact is local to applications that expose or misuse the manual
`acquire_*` / `release_*` APIs. If the lock protects integrity-sensitive
mutable state, wrong-thread write release can allow concurrent writers
and data races. The stray read-release path can cause denial of service
by corrupting the lock counter.

### Credit

Pranjali Thakur - depthfirst ([depthfirst.com](<http://depthfirst.com>))

advisory.title: Deeply nested CSS blocks and functions can trigger a SystemStackError or excessive memory usage
advisory.description:
## Impact

Crass recursively parses CSS simple blocks and functions without a
depth guard. An attacker-controlled value containing many deeply
nested blocks can recurse until Ruby raises SystemStackError:
stack level too deep, or can cause excessive memory usage.

advisory.title: Large numeric exponents cause CPU and memory denial of service
advisory.description:
## Impact

Crass converts CSS scientific notation number values with unbounded
exponentiation before it clamps the result to Float::MAX. Applications
that use Crass to parse attacker-controlled CSS strings can be forced
to spend disproportionate CPU and memory parsing a tiny input,
possibly resulting in a crash.

Exponents are now bounded before 10**exponent is computed.

advisory.title: Non-ASCII characters cause superlinear CPU consumption
advisory.description:
## Impact

When parsing an input containing non-ASCII characters, inefficiencies
in how Crass tracks the positions of multi-byte characters result
in superlinear parsing time. An attacker-controlled input consisting
of many non-ASCII characters could cause excessive CPU consumption
and potentially denial of service.

advisory.title: Incorrect tokenization of bad URLs enables CSS sanitizer bypass
advisory.description:
## Summary

Crass's tokenizer didn't terminate a bad URL token at a ) that followed
an escaped backslash (\\). As a result, Crass consumed more input as
part of the bad URL than a spec-compliant browser does. CSS sanitizers
that parse untrusted CSS with Crass and re-emit it could be tricked
into passing through declarations, style rules, or at-rules (including
@import) that the sanitizer would otherwise have removed, but that
a browser would then parse and apply.

## Impact

Crass by itself only mis-tokenizes input. The security impact is on
CSS sanitizers that use Crass to make allow/deny decisions and then
re-serialize the CSS. Exploitation requires a sanitizer that doesn't
reject bad URL tokens wherever they occur. Confirmed examples:

- Sanitize (all versions through 7.0.0): Sanitize::CSS.properties,
  style attributes, Sanitize::CSS.stylesheet, and <style> elements.
- Loofah (Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css, used for style attributes),
  and therefore rails-html-sanitizer (sanitize_css, and sanitize when
  style is a permitted attribute).

advisory.title: A large number of adjacent CSS comments can trigger a SystemStackError
advisory.description:
## Impact

When the :preserve_comments option is not enabled (which is the
default behavior), Crass discards CSS comments by recursively
consuming the next token. An attacker who provides a stylesheet
containing a very large number of adjacent comments can cause
excessive recursion and trigger a SystemStackError.

advisory.title: SVG `<textPath>` and `<mpath>` bypass local-reference restriction in Loofah
advisory.description:
## Summary

Loofah restricts `href` and `xlink:href` on certain SVG elements to
same-document references. Two elements escaped the restriction:

- `<textPath>`: `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF` listed it in lowercase as `textpath`,
  but the HTML5 parser names the element `textPath` inside `<svg>`, so the
  check never matched on the HTML5 path.
- `<mpath>`: absent from `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so its references were never
  restricted on either path.

`rails-html-sanitizer` reuses this safelist in its `PermitScrubber`, so it is
affected too.

## Impact

An external `href` or `xlink:href` on `<textPath>` or `<mpath>` survives
sanitization. Firefox fetches the URL when rendering the content, which leaks
the viewer's IP address, user agent, and referrer, and can reach hosts
routable only from the viewer's network. Chrome and WebKit do not fetch
external references on these elements. The impact is a network request to an
attacker-chosen URL, not script execution.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied SVG, directly or inside HTML, with
Loofah's default allowlist or with `rails-html-sanitizer` with SVG elements
permitted are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

advisory.title: Loofah `allowed_uri?` does not detect `javascript:` URIs split by numeric character references without semicolons
advisory.description:
## Summary

Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri? does not correctly reject javascript:
or vbscript: URIs when the scheme is split by a numeric character
reference that has no trailing semicolon. A browser decodes such
references and resolves the URL to an executable javascript: scheme,
while allowed_uri? reports it safe.

This is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-46fp-8f5p-pf2m, which handled
numeric character references with a trailing ; (	, 
, )
but did not cover the forms without semicolons.

## Impact

Callers that validate a user-controlled URL with
Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri? and then render the approved value
into an href or other browser-interpreted URI attribute may be
vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS). This includes applications
that call allowed_uri? directly, as well as higher-level features
built on top of it, such as Action Text 8.2's markdown link validation.

## Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @MoonFuji.

advisory.title: Loofah `allowed_uri?` does not detect `javascript:` URIs split by named whitespace character references
advisory.description:
## Summary

Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri? does not correctly reject javascript:
URIs when the scheme is split or prefixed by the HTML5 named character
references 	 (tab) or 
 (line feed).

This is a bypass of the fix for GHSA-46fp-8f5p-pf2m, which handled
the equivalent numeric character references (	, 
, ) but
did not cover the named forms.

advisory.title: SVG `href` attribute bypasses local-reference restriction in Loofah
advisory.description:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 sanitizer restricted only the xlink:href attribute on
certain SVG elements to local, same-document references. Browsers
also accept a plain href attribute as an alternative to the deprecated
xlink:href per the SVG 2 spec, but Loofah did not apply the same
restriction to it, allowing those elements to reference arbitrary
external documents.

## Impact

SVG <use> can load and render external SVG content by reference. If
the referenced external SVG is same-origin and contains scripts or
other dangerous content, it could execute in the context of the
sanitized document. <feImage> can load external images, which can be
used for tracking. Modern browsers restrict cross-origin <use>
fetches, which limits but does not eliminate the risk.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied SVG (directly, or as part
of HTML) with Loofah's default allowlist are affected.

## Credit

Found by the maintainer, Mike Dalessio, during a security audit.

advisory.title: Mutation XSS in Loofah HTML5 scrubbers through unescaped attribute values
advisory.description:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 scrubbers could emit output that a browser parses into
different markup, allowing mutation XSS. Nokogiri < 1.19.5 did not escape `<`
and `>` in attribute values. When the output contained certain MathML, a
browser treated markup inside an allowed attribute as live HTML. The `:strip`
scrubber is affected in every browser. The `:prune` and `:escape` scrubbers
are affected in WebKit browsers such as Safari.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes `<` and `>` in attribute values, as the HTML standard
requires. Loofah 2.25.3 requires Nokogiri >= 1.19.5.

## Impact

Applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with Loofah's HTML5 API
(`Loofah.html5_fragment`, `Loofah.html5_document` and the `scrub_html5_*`
methods) and display the result to other people are affected, including with
the default allowlist.

Not affected: Loofah's HTML4 API (including `Loofah::Helpers.sanitize`), the
`:whitewash` scrubber, rails-html-sanitizer's default configuration, and
JRuby.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3, or upgrade Nokogiri to >= 1.19.5.

advisory.title: CSS url() sanitization bypass via escaped parentheses in Loofah
advisory.description:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.scrub_css` rejected any property whose top-level Crass
tokens included a `:url` or `:bad_url`, and left `url` out of the allowed CSS
functions. Both checks ran only against the first parse of the `style`
attribute. When `scrub_css` rebuilt each property it emitted identifiers with
their CSS escapes decoded, so parentheses written as escapes — `url\28 …\29` —
hid the `url` token from the checks, and the rebuilt value was re-parsed into
a live `url()` that nothing checked again. An escaped property name, six-digit
escapes, escaped comments and escaped quotes all reached the same place.

## Impact

A sanitized `style` attribute could make a viewer's browser issue a request to
an attacker-chosen URL. `list-style` fetches on render with no interaction,
`cursor` on hover. That leaks the viewer's IP address, user agent and access
timing, and can reach hosts routable only from the viewer's network. No script
survives sanitization and the attacker cannot read the response, so the
request itself is the whole impact.

Applications that sanitize user-supplied HTML with Loofah's default allowlist
and display it to other people are affected.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Reported by NotAFlightRisk through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting.

advisory.title: Regular expression denial of service in Loofah's SVG local-reference check
advisory.description:
## Summary

Loofah's HTML5 sanitizer restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes of
SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the attribute
value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line start and
`\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine rescan the
value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its length.

CRuby 3.1 and earlier, and JRuby, are affected. CRuby 3.2 added linear-time
regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear. JRuby's regexp engine does
not.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of
proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href`
or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

The default safelist allows the elements in `SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF`, so no
configuration change is required.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3. Applications on CRuby that cannot upgrade should
run CRuby 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time.

## References

- [CWE-1333: Inefficient Regular Expression
  Complexity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1333.html)
- [Ruby 3.2.0 release
  notes](https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2022/12/25/ruby-3-2-0-released/)

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

advisory.title: Loofah allowed_uri? treats javascript&#x3a alert(1) as safe
advisory.description:
## Summary

`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` returns `true` for a `javascript:` or
`vbscript:` URI whose scheme is split by a numeric character reference without
a trailing semicolon, followed by a character that `allowed_uri?` strips, such
as a space or tab. A browser ends the reference at that character and reads
`javascript&#x3a alert(1)` as `javascript: alert(1)`.

## Details

`allowed_uri?` strips control characters and whitespace before it decodes
numeric character references. Removing the character that ends a
semicolon-less reference lets the reference run on into the following text, so
`&#x3a alert` decodes as `&#x3aa` (U+03AA) instead of a colon, and no scheme
is detected. The same applies to decimal references and to references that
encode a scheme letter, as in `&#x6a\tavascript:alert(1)`.

Loofah's default `sanitize()` path is **not** affected, because Nokogiri
decodes the entity during parsing before Loofah evaluates the URI. This issue
affects only callers of the public `allowed_uri?` string-level helper that
pass it HTML-encoded strings.

## Impact

Applications that validate a user-controlled URL with
`Loofah::HTML5::Scrub.allowed_uri?` and then render the approved value into an
`href` or another browser-interpreted URI attribute may be vulnerable to
cross-site scripting. `Rails::HTML::Sanitizer.allowed_uri?` re-exports the
same helper.

## Mitigation

Upgrade to Loofah >= 2.25.3.

## Credit

Responsibly reported by GitHub user @manus-pi.

advisory.title: Email address spoofing via malformed RFC 2047 encoded-words in mail
advisory.description:
## Summary

Mail::Utilities.q_value_decode and Mail::Utilities.b_value_decode
decoded only the first RFC 2047 encoded-word in a string and used
an overly greedy pattern to match the charset token. A crafted,
malformed encoded-word embedded in an address display name or local
part could cause the decoded output to differ from what a human
reviewer or downstream parser would expect, allowing an attacker
to spoof the apparent sender/recipient address.

advisory.title: msgpack-ruby JRuby decoder makes uncapped header-count allocations; a 5-byte message forces multi-GiB OOM
advisory.description:
### Summary

The **JRuby** implementation of msgpack (`msgpack` gem,
`java` platform — pure Java decoder under `ext/java/`) sizes containers
directly from the element count written in the message header, with
**no cap at all**: no equivalent of the C unpacker's `SHRT_MAX` clamp
(since 1.7.3) and none of the buffered-bytes cap that commit c8d42d8
added for CRuby in 1.8.6. A single 5-byte message decides how much
memory a JVM process tries to allocate:

* `array32` header declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` elements → `new
  IRubyObject[0x7FFFFFFF]` (~8 GiB of reference slots) attempted
  immediately → `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Requested array size
  exceeds VM limit`.

* Counts *below* the VM's max-array-size but above available heap
  (e.g. 5×10⁸ with a 512 MiB heap) produce a **real allocation attempt**
  — `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` — the JVM genuinely tries to
  take the memory before failing.

* `str32`/`bin32` headers declaring `0x7FFFFFFF` bytes do the same
  via `readBytes(size)` → `new byte[size]`.

* Below the failure threshold there is a **silent band**: one streaming
  unpacker fed only an `array32` header with count 2×10⁷ (5 wire bytes,
  zero elements) grows used heap **+78 MiB immediately**, no exception
  (`each` swallows the underflow), and the footprint stays elevated
  after `Unpacker#reset` + full GC. Linear in declared count
  (~4 B/element); nothing bounds it — not delivered bytes, not a
  per-container cap.

Only counts ≥ 2³¹ are refused (a clean `MessagePack::UnderflowError`
from `getUnsignedInt()`), and only **maps** are safe (`consumeHash`
grows per element instead of pre-sizing). Verified on the released
gem `msgpack 1.8.6 java`, JRuby 9.4.12 / OpenJDK 25, 2026-10-30 —
i.e. **unfixed in the current release**. Proposed fix mirrors
c8d42d8: cap initial allocation by bytes actually buffered and
grow as data arrives; read strings in bounded chunks instead of
allocating the declared length up front.

### Impact

**Type.** Uncontrolled resource consumption driven by *declared* sizes
rather than delivered bytes — CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without
Limits or Throttling), precisely CWE-1325 (Independent Resource Usage
Limiting Not Applied). Availability only; no confidentiality/integrity
impact, no code execution.

**Who is impacted.** Any JRuby application that feeds untrusted msgpack
to `MessagePack.unpack`/`Unpacker` — the java-platform gem's whole
user base (JRuby-based services, log/RPC pipelines, JVM polyglot
stacks using this gem). For them: remote OOM of a shared-heap JVM
from a 5-byte message, or silent heap spend below the exception band.

advisory.title: DFVULN-839 - Use-After-Free in MessagePack::Buffer#clear Enables Cross-Buffer Disclosure
advisory.description:
## Summary

MessagePack::Buffer#clear shifts out every chunk and returns its
4 KiB rmem page to the shared pool, but does not reset the buffer's
rmem cursor (rmem_last, rmem_end, rmem_owner). The next write sees
"unused rmem space" left over from the freed page and hands back a
slice of memory that has already been returned to the pool. A second
MessagePack::Buffer then re-acquires that same page, so reading the
cleared-and-rewritten buffer discloses the second buffer's bytes — a
same-process use-after-free with cross-buffer information
disclosure (and the symmetric write-corruption).

advisory.title: Net::IMAP: Command Injection via non-synchronizing literal in "raw" argument
advisory.description:
Several Net::IMAP commands accept a "raw data" argument that is sent
verbatim after validation to prevent command injection.  However,
if a server does not support non-synchronizing literals, it may
still be possible to inject arbitrary IMAP commands inside
non-synchronizing literals.

### Details

Raw data arguments support embedded literal values, both synchronizing
and non-synchronizing.  Non-synchronizing literals can only be safely
sent when the server advertises any of the `LITERAL+`, `LITERAL-`, or
`IMAP4rev2` capabilities.  But raw data arguments do not verify server
support for non-synchronizing literals prior to sending.

Servers without support for non-synchronizing literals could handle
them in several different ways:  If a server sees a `"}\r\n"` byte
sequence but can't parse the literal bytesize, it _may_ cautiously
decide to close the connection, blocking any command injection attacks.
However, a server without support for non-synchronizing literals may
instead interpret the `"+}\r\n"` as the end of a malformed command
line and respond with a tagged `BAD`.  In that case, the contents
of the literal will be interpreted as one or more new pipelined
commands, allowing a CRLF command injection attack to succeed.

This affects the following commands' string arguments:
* `criteria` for `#search` and `#uid_search`
* `search_keys` for `#sort`, `#thread`, `#uid_sort`, and `#uid_thread`
* `attr` for `#fetch` and `#uid_fetch`

Prior to `net-imap` v0.6.4, v0.5.14, and v0.4.24, raw data arguments
were not validated in _any_ way, so they were also vulnerable to
this attack.  See CVE-2026-42257 (GHSA-hm49-wcqc-g2xg).

### Impact

Fortunately, `LITERAL-` is supported by most modern IMAP servers.  Even
without support for non-synchronizing literals, cautious servers may
handle invalid literal bytesize by closing the connection .  However,
servers which handle a non-synchronizing literal just like any other
malformed command will enable this vulnerability.

If a developer passes an unvalidated user-controlled input for one
of these method arguments, an attacker can append CRLF sequence
followed by a new IMAP command (like DELETE mailbox). Although this
does not directly enable data exfiltration, it could be combined with
other attack vectors or knowledge of the target system's attributes,
e.g.: shared mail folders or the application's installed response handlers.

### Mitigation

Update to a version of `net-imap` which validates server support
for non-synchronizing literals before sending them.

If upgrading `net-imap` is not possible:
* Explicitly validate user-controlled inputs to prevent embedded
  non-synchronizing literals unless the server supports them.
* For a simpler, more cautious approach: all embedded literals can
  be unconditionally prohibited, by checking that string inputs
  do not contain any CR or LF bytes.
* Verify that the server advertises any of the `LITERAL+`, `LITERAL-`,
  or `IMAP4rev2` capabilities before using untrusted string inputs
  for the affected "raw data" arguments.

advisory.title: Net::IMAP: Denial of Service via incomplete raw argument validation
advisory.description:
### Summary

Several Net::IMAP commands accept a raw string argument which is only
validated to prevent CRLF injection and then sent verbatim.  If this
string is derived from user-controlled input, an attacker can force
the next command to be absorbed as a continuation of the first command.
This will cause the first command to eventually fail, but also prevents
 it from returning until another command is sent (from another thread).
That other command will not return until the connection is closed.

### Details

`Net::IMAP::RawData` was hardened in v0.6.4, v0.5.14, and v0.4.24 to
reject string arguments that would smuggle an invalid literal-continuation
marker onto the wire (CVE-2026-42257, GHSA-hm49-wcqc-g2xg).  But the
trailing-marker check uses an incorrect regex which does not match
`{0}` or `{0+}`, so an attacker-controlled seach `criteria` or fetch
`attr` string ending in `{0}` or `{0+}` passes validation and is sent
verbatim.  Since these arguments are sent as the last argument in the
command, they will be followed by CRLF.  Although the CRLF was intended
to end the command, the server will interpret it as part of a literal
prefix.  This consumes the next command the client puts on the socket
as additional arguments to the current command.

This affects the following command's arguments:
  * `criteria` for `#search` and `#uid_search`
  * `search_keys` for `#sort`, `#thread`, `#uid_sort`, and `#uid_thread`
  * `attr` for `#fetch` and `#uid_fetch`

The command which contained the attacker's raw data will not be able
to complete until the _next_ command is issued.  If commands are only
sent from single thread, the first command will hang until the connection
times out (most likely by the server closing the connection).

If a second command is sent _(from another thread)_, this would allow
the server to respond to the first command.  This combined command
_will_ be invalid:
  * The `{0}\\r\\n` literal prohibits other arguments (such as a quoted
    string) from spanning both commands
  * It will be sent without the space delimiter which is required
    between arguments.
  * The second command's tag will not be a valid argument to any of the
   vulnerable commands.

So the server _should_ respond to the first command with a `BAD` response,
which will raise a `BadResponseError`.

But, since the server never saw a second command, the second command will
never receive a tagged response and the thread that sent it will hang until
the connection is closed.

### Impact

This will result in unexpected crashes and timeouts, which could be used
to create a simple denial of service attack.  This attack will present
very similarly to common network issues or server issues which also result
in commands hanging or unexpectedly raising exceptions. By itself, this
does not allow command injection.  But the confusion caused by these
errors could lead to other downstream issues, especially in a
multi-threaded environment.

### Mitigation

Update to a patched version of `net-imap` which validates that `RawData`
arguments may not end with literal continuation markers.
If `net-imap` cannot be upgraded:\n* Validate that user input to the
affected command arguments does not end with `\"}\"`.
* Use of `Timeout` or other standard strategies for slow connections
  and misbehaving servers will also mitigate the effects of this.

### Extra caution is required when issuing commands from multiple threads.

While `net-imap` does have rudimentary support for issuing commands
from multiple threads, the user is responsible for synchronizing that
commands are issued in a logically coherent order, and for ensuring
that commands are only pipelined when it is safe to do so.

Practically, this means that many commands cannot be safely pipelined together,
and user code will often need to wait for state changing commands to successfully
complete before issuing commands that rely on that state change.

advisory.title: Net::IMAP: Command Injection via ID command argument
advisory.description:
### Summary

Two `Net::IMAP` commands, `#id` and `#enable`, do not validate their
arguments.  Arguments to either command could be used by an attacker
to inject arbitrary IMAP commands.

Please note that passing untrusted inputs to these commands is usually
inappropriate and expected to be uncommon.

### Details

When `Net::IMAP#id` is called with a hash argument, although the ID
field value strings are correctly quoted (escaping quoted specials),
they were not validated to prohibit CRLF sequences.

While `Net::IMAP#enable` does process its arguments for aliases, it
does not validate them as valid atoms (or as a list of valid atoms).
The `#to_s` value is sent verbatim.

### Impact

This is expected to impact very few users: use of untrusted user input
for either command is expected to be very uncommon.

The documentation for `#enable` explicitly warns that using any arguments
that are not in the explicitly supported list may result in undocumented
behavior.  Using arbitrary untrusted user input for `#enable` will always
be inappropriate.

Although client ID field values will most commonly be static and hardcoded,
dynamic input sources may be used.  For example, client ID fields may be
set by configuration or version numbers.  Using untrusted user inputs
for client ID fields is expected to be uncommon.  But any untrusted
inputs to client ID can trivially exploit this vulnerability.

Untrusted inputs to either command may include a CRLF sequence followed
by a new IMAP command (like DELETE mailbox). Although this does not
directly enable data exfiltration, it could be combined with other
attack vectors or knowledge of the target system's attributes,
e.g.: shared mail folders or the application's installed response handlers.

### Mitigation

Update to a version of `net-imap` which validates `#id` and `#enable`
arguments.

Untrusted inputs should _never_ be used for `#enable` arguments.

If `net-imap` cannot be upgraded:
* do not use untrusted inputs for client ID field values
* or add validation that client ID field values must not contain
  any CR or LF bytes.

advisory.title: Use-After-Free in Nokogiri when replacing an attribute value
advisory.description:
### Summary

Nokogiri's CRuby native extension could leave a Ruby wrapper pointing to freed
memory when replacing the value of an existing XML attribute via
`Nokogiri::XML::Node#[]=` or `Nokogiri::XML::Node#lang=`. If Ruby code had
already accessed the attribute's child nodes, replacing the value could free
those native child nodes while their wrappers remained reachable. Using one of
those child nodes afterwards could cause an invalid read and a possible
segfault.

This is the same class of issue as
[GHSA-phwj-rprq-35pp](https://github.com/sparklemotion/nokogiri/security/advisories/GHSA-phwj-rprq-35pp),
which was fixed for `Attr#value=` in Nokogiri 1.19.4.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 preserves all already-wrapped attribute child nodes before
replacing the attribute value.

JRuby is not affected.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity. Reaching it
requires an unusual API-usage pattern that does not arise during normal use.
The application must directly access an attribute's child nodes and then
replace that same attribute's value via `Node#[]=` or `Node#lang=`. Nokogiri
1.19.5 makes this pattern safe with no change to the public API.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later.

As a workaround, avoid accessing attribute child nodes directly via
`Attr#children` or similar before replacing the same attribute's value.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by zx (@manus-pi).

advisory.title: Possible Mutation XSS when serializing `noscript` content in `Nokogiri::HTML5` documents
advisory.description:
### Summary

Nokogiri's HTML5 serializer did not escape text inside `noscript` elements, or
`<` and `>` inside attribute values. When a document parsed with the default
options is serialized, a browser with scripting enabled can parse the output
into markup that Nokogiri's parser never produced. This is a mutation XSS for
applications that sanitize untrusted HTML with `Nokogiri::HTML5`, allow
`noscript` elements, and send the serialized output to browsers.

Nokogiri 1.19.5 escapes both, as the HTML standard's serialization algorithm
requires. Text inside `noscript` is still emitted unescaped for documents
parsed with `parse_noscript_content_as_text: true`.

Only the C extension (CRuby and TruffleRuby) is affected. JRuby does not
implement `Nokogiri::HTML5`.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity (CVSS 2.3,
`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:P/VC:N/VI:N/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N`).
Exploitation requires an application that allows `noscript` in sanitized HTML.
Loofah and rails-html-sanitizer do not allow it by default, and Sanitize
always removes it.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.5 or later.

Applications that sanitize HTML and allow `noscript` should parse with
`parse_noscript_content_as_text: true` (available since Nokogiri 1.17.0), or
remove `noscript` elements. This is the workaround for earlier versions, and
it is recommended on every version: some content inside `noscript` is
serialized unchanged, as the standard requires.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by @a-zara-n.

advisory.title: Nokogiri: Possible Out-of-Bounds Read in `Nokogiri::XML::NodeSet#[]`
advisory.description:
### Summary

`Nokogiri::XML::NodeSet#[]` (and its alias `#slice`) checked the requested
index against the node set's bounds using a 32-bit-truncated copy of the
index. A large negative index could pass the check and then be used at full
width, reading outside the node set's storage. On CRuby this is an
out-of-bounds read that typically crashes the process; on JRuby it is not
memory-unsafe but returns an incorrect node.

Nokogiri 1.19.4 performs the bounds check against the full-width index.

### Severity
