### Summary

XInclude substitution performed by `Nokogiri::XML::Node#do_xinclude` replaced
each `<xi:include>` in place, freeing the include node along with its children
(such as `<xi:fallback>` and its descendants) and any namespaces declared on
them. If an application had already exposed one of those nodes or namespaces
to Ruby, the corresponding Ruby object was left pointing at freed memory.
Using the object could result in invalid reads or writes to memory.

Nokogiri 1.19.4 substitutes each `<xi:include>` on a defensive copy by
default, so the structures libxml2 frees are never the ones bound to live Ruby
objects.

Only the CRuby implementation is affected; JRuby is not affected.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity. Reaching it
requires an unusual API-usage pattern that does not arise during normal use.
The application must parse a document without XInclude, traverse into an
`<xi:include>` subtree to expose its nodes or namespaces to Ruby, and only
then invoke XInclude processing. The common case, requesting XInclude at parse
time, operates on a freshly parsed document whose nodes are not yet exposed to
Ruby and is not affected. Nokogiri 1.19.4 makes this pattern safe by default
and requires no change to application code.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.4 or later.

As a workaround for earlier versions, perform XInclude substitution at parse
time (with the `xinclude` parse option) rather than calling `#do_xinclude` on
a document that has already been traversed. A freshly parsed document has no
nodes exposed to Ruby, so the substitution is safe.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Zheng Yu from depthfirst.com.

advisory.title: Nokogiri: Possible Use-After-Free when setting `Document#root=` to an invalid node type
advisory.description:
### Summary

`Nokogiri::XML::Document#root=` validated only that the new root was a
`Nokogiri::XML::Node`, allowing a DTD node to be set as the document root. The
result is a heap use-after-free during garbage collection or finalization,
leading to an invalid memory read or potentially a segfault.

Nokogiri 1.19.4 restricts `Document#root=` to element nodes, raising
`TypeError` for any other node type.

This memory-safety issue affects only the CRuby implementation (libxml2). The
JRuby implementation was not affected; the same input validation was added
there for behavioral parity.

### Severity

The Nokogiri maintainers have evaluated this as low severity. This is only
triggered by a programming error. It requires application code to assign a
non-element node such as a DTD as the document root via `Document#root=`.
Nokogiri 1.19.4 now raises `TypeError` instead of allowing a use-after-free.
It cannot be triggered by untrusted input or through normal use of the public
API.

### Mitigation

Upgrade to Nokogiri 1.19.4 or later.

As a workaround, applications that cannot upgrade should avoid assigning a DTD
(or any non-element node) via `Document#root=`.

### Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Zheng Yu from depthfirst.com.

advisory.title: Memory exhaustion with SSL connections
advisory.description:
## Impact

An unauthenticated client can cause excessive memory use in a Puma
process with an SSL binding, with no limit, until first_data_timeout
closes the connection.

When OpenSSL hits a fatal error while reading a TLS record, Puma's
MiniSSL C extension checks SSL_want_read() before SSL_get_error(),
so it treats the fatal error as "need more data". Puma then keeps
passing everything the client sends to OpenSSL's input buffer,
which is never read again.

This is not present on unencrypted (UNIX, TCP) Puma binds. A plaintext
listener closes a connection that sends more than 112 KB without
a complete request.

## What configurations are affected

Deployments on MRI where Puma uses ssl:// or ssl_bind:

* ssl_bind "0.0.0.0", "9292", cert: "/path/to/cert.pem", key: "/path/to/key.pem"

The default configuration, which binds plain TCP, is not affected.
JRuby uses a separate TLS implementation.

advisory.title: pumactl does not verify the TLS identity of SSL control servers
advisory.description:
## Impact

An attacker on the network path between pumactl and a Puma control
server reached over ssl:// can steal the control token and use it
to stop, restart, or inspect Puma.

pumactl support for ssl:// control URLs was added in v4.3.0 (#2052).

When pumactl connects to an ssl:// control URL, it accepts any TLS
certificate. It should check that a trusted authority issued the
certificate and that the certificate matches the hostname in the URL.
An attacker who can intercept or redirect the connection can present
their own certificate, and pumactl then sends them the control token.

With the token, the attacker can send authenticated commands to the
real control server, including stop, restart, and stats.

Only deployments that run pumactl against an ssl:// control URL
are affected, for example:

  * pumactl --control-url 'ssl://control.example.com:9293'
    --control-token "$PUMA_CONTROL_TOKEN" stats

Puma's default configuration is not affected. The control server
is off by default, and unix:// control URLs are not affected.

## Acknowledgements

Thanks to @ahmedehab-nopr for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Graceful shutdown waits indefinitely on trickled request bodies
advisory.description:
## Impact

Puma servers running in single mode with the default force_shutdown_after
:forever can be prevented from shutting down or restarting by an
unauthenticated client.

When Puma begins a graceful shutdown, it hands any request that is
still being received to the thread pool so that it can finish. The
thread pool then waits for that request with no deadline. Puma's
read timeout restarts every time a byte arrives, so an attacker who
sends a POST with a large Content-Length and then trickles one body
byte every few seconds can keep that request "in progress" for as
long as they like. The same works with chunked bodies and with
trickled headers. Puma stops accepting new connections, but the
process does not exit until the attacker closes the socket.

This delays or blocks deploys, restarts, and operational recovery.
Process supervisors that eventually send SIGKILL will end the
process, but any other in-flight requests are lost when they do.
Many trickling connections can be used together; each holds a
file descriptor but uses very little memory.

Deployments using Puma's default single-mode configuration are affected.

Unaffected:

* Cluster mode (workers N) bounds the delay: the master kills a
  stuck worker after worker_shutdown_timeout (30 seconds by default).

* A finite force_shutdown_after bounds the delay.

* Deployments behind a proxy that buffers request bodies before
  forwarding them are not affected. For example, nginx's default
  proxy_request_buffering on keeps a trickled body from reaching Puma.

## Acknowledgements

Thanks to Zheng Yu of depthfirst (@cla7aye15I4nd) for reporting
this issue and providing a proposed fix.

advisory.title: Reactor timeout queue loses order, letting a slow client keep other connections open past their timeout
advisory.description:
## Impact

An unauthenticated client can stop Puma from closing other connections
when their first_data_timeout or persistent_timeout expires.

The reactor keeps waiting connections in a queue sorted by deadline.
Puma sorted the queue only when new connections arrived, but it
extended a connection's deadline every time that connection sent
data. A client that connects and then sends about one byte per
timeout interval, without completing its request, stays at the
front of the queue with a deadline that is always in the future.
Every expired connection behind it stays open for as long as the
client keeps sending, or until a new connection arrives and causes a sort.

Connections held this way cost Puma one file descriptor and a small
amount of memory each. Puma does not crash, and the effect ends
when the slow client stops or new traffic arrives.
This bug was introduced in v5.0.3 by the reactor refactor (#2279).

The default configuration is affected.

## Acknowledgements

Thanks to @0xMigoo for the report and the controlled proof of
concept that isolated the missing sort.

advisory.title: ssl_cipher_filter values containing `+` are decoded to a wider cipher list
advisory.description:
## Impact

Puma servers that set an ssl_cipher_filter containing + accept TLS
cipher suites that the filter is meant to exclude. Any client that
can reach the SSL listener can negotiate those suites.

Support for ssl_cipher_filter in ssl:// bind URLs was added in
v3.12.0 (#1478), and in the ssl_bind DSL in v4.0.0 (#1676).

In an OpenSSL cipher string, + means "both": AES+SHA selects suites
that are AES and SHA. Puma decodes the query of a bind URL as HTML
form data, where + means a space, and a space in a cipher string
means "either". So the filter !aNULL:AES+SHA, which is the example
in Puma's README, reaches OpenSSL as !aNULL:AES SHA: every AES
suite plus every SHA suite. On OpenSSL 3.x that is 94 suites in
place of 27, including suites without forward secrecy.

Puma logs nothing, and the startup output shows the filter as written,
so operators cannot see that their filter is not applied. The filter
only gets wider: explicit exclusions such as !aNULL or !3DES still apply.

Deployments that set ssl_cipher_filter with a + are affected, in either form:

* ssl_bind "0.0.0.0", "9292", ssl_cipher_filter: "!aNULL:AES+SHA",
  cert: "...", key: "..."

* puma -b 'ssl://0.0.0.0:9292?key=...&cert=...&ssl_cipher_filter=!aNULL:AES+SHA'

The default configuration is not affected. Filters without +,
ssl_ciphersuites (TLS 1.3), and JRuby's ssl_cipher_list are not affected.

## Acknowledgements

Thanks to @b84330808 for reporting this issue.

advisory.title: Accept loop retries without pausing when out of file descriptors, flooding the log
advisory.description:
## Impact

An unauthenticated client can make Puma:

1. write log lines as fast as it can...
2. ...which eventually may fill the disk...
3. ...and when the disk fills, Puma will stop accepting connections.

The client can do this by opening enough idle connections to use up
the process's file descriptors.

When accept fails because the process is out of file descriptors
(EMFILE), the connection stays in the listen backlog, so the listening
socket stays readable. Puma logs the error and calls accept again
at once, with no pause. Each attempt fails the same way and writes
another "Listen loop" error line. An attacker who opens about as
many idle connections as the file descriptor limit, and sends
nothing on them, keeps Puma in this loop. The attacker reconnects
when Puma closes idle connections after first_data_timeout, so
the loop does not end.

If the log destination then raises an error, such as ENOSPC when
the disk is full, that error escapes the listen loop and ends
the thread that accepts connections.

Deployments that accept connections directly from clients are
affected, including the default configuration.

Deployments behind a reverse proxy or load balancer that limits
connections to Puma are not affected, because the client cannot
open enough connections to Puma itself.

## Acknowledgements

Found by Puma's maintainers during an internal security review.

advisory.title: JRuby HTTP parser lets request headers change the request path and query string, bypassing proxy URL rules
advisory.description:
## Impact

On JRuby, an unauthenticated client can use request headers to
change Rack env keys that Puma should build only from the request
line, such as QUERY_STRING and PATH_INFO.

If an application behind a proxy, WAF, or other firewall that makes
decisions based on the request line, this could be abused so that
the app can receive a different path or query. Examples might include
rules like: "only certain IPs can reach /admin", "URLs must be
correctly signed", or "URLs must not match this pattern of a known attacker".

Examples:

* GET /search?q=x with Query-String: &role=admin: WAF sees the query
  string as q=x, but Rack parses the params as {"q"=>"x, ", "role"=>"admin"}.

* GET http://example.com/public HTTP/1.1 (absolute-form) with
  Request-Path: /admin: WAF or proxy sees /public, but Rack thinks
 PATH_INFO is /admin.

advisory.title: Client that stops reading a TLS or file response holds a worker thread indefinitely
advisory.description:
## Impact

An unauthenticated client can hold a Puma worker thread indefinitely
when Puma sends it a TLS response, or a file response larger than
64 KB. With enough connections, it can take the server offline.

The client sends a request and then stops reading the response.
Puma's write timeout (10 seconds) should then free the worker
thread. In two cases it never fires, and the thread stays blocked
until the client disconnects:

* TLS: MiniSSL::Socket#write_nonblock performs a blocking write.
  This has been the case since v3.9.0 (#1274).

* File bodies over 64 KB, on any bind: Puma sends File bodies, and
  bodies that respond to to_path, with IO.copy_stream, which has no
  write timeout. This has been the case since v6.0.0 (#2896).
  Rack::Files, Rails static file serving, and Rails send_file return
  these bodies.

An attacker who opens max_threads such connections per worker leaves
no threads to serve requests. The attack needs very little bandwidth
and no CPU on the server.

Two kinds of deployment are affected:

* Deployments where Puma terminates TLS itself, with an ssl://
  bind or ssl_bind:

  * ssl_bind "0.0.0.0", "9292", cert: "/path/to/cert.pem", key:
    "/path/to/key.pem"

* Applications that serve a file larger than 64 KB through Puma, on
  any bind. Puma's default configuration is affected in this case.

Deployments behind a proxy that buffers responses are not affected
for files that fit in the proxy's buffer. nginx buffers by default
(proxy_buffering on), up to 1 GB per response in a temporary file.

## Acknowledgements

Thanks to @wtn and @SounLabs, who reported this issue
independently, and to @wtn for the fix.

advisory.title: Reactor blocks on `100 Continue` writes to clients that stop reading, stalling other connections
advisory.description:
## Impact

An unauthenticated client with one connection per worker process can
stop Puma from serving every connection that waits in the reactor,
for as long as it holds that connection open.

Each Puma worker has one reactor thread, which holds connections
waiting for more data: keep-alive connections between requests,
requests that arrive in more than one read, and TLS connections
still in the handshake. When a request with Expect: 100-continue
completes its headers on the reactor thread, Puma writes the
HTTP/1.1 100 Continue interim response with a blocking write and
no timeout. An attacker pipelines a request for a large response
before the Expect: 100-continue request and does not read that
response. The server's send buffer for the connection fills, and
the reactor thread blocks on the 25-byte interim write until the
attacker reads or closes. The 408 Request Timeout response and
error responses for requests that fail to parse in the reactor
were written from the reactor thread in the same way.

While the reactor thread is blocked, Puma does not read from or
time out any connection in the reactor on that worker. Requests
that arrive complete in a single read are still served, so the
server appears to hang only for some clients.

The default configuration is affected (queue_requests is on by
default) when Puma is directly reachable by clients and the
application has a route whose response size the client can
influence. A reverse proxy in front of Puma that buffers
responses prevents the attack.

## Acknowledgements

Thanks to @wtn for the report, the TCP and Unix socket proofs
of concept, the note about the 408 path, and the original fix.

advisory.title: Rack::Request#host_with_port and `#base_url` return an invalid `Host` verbatim, enabling URL and allowlist bypass
advisory.description:
Rack::Request#host_with_port, and therefore #base_url and #url,
return the raw authority string when it fails validation. An
attacker-controlled Host, X-Forwarded-Host, or Forwarded:
host= value containing characters that are not permitted in an
authority is embedded verbatim in URLs generated by the application.

This completes the fix for CVE-2026-34835 (GHSA-g2pf-xv49-m2h5),
which made #host and #hostname return nil for an invalid authority
but left this path unchanged.

## Impact

Applications that build absolute URLs, redirects, or origin-dependent
checks from req.url, req.base_url, or req.host_with_port, and that
do not enforce a host allowlist, may emit URLs containing attacker-chosen
characters such as @, /, ?, #, spaces, or angle brackets. Generated
links and Location headers can be redirected through userinfo tricks,
string-based URL checks can be bypassed, and markup is reflected
where the application does not escape the value. For example, redirect
in Sinatra behind a proxy that forwards X-Forwarded-Host emits the
raw invalid authority in Location.

Rails overrides these methods in Action Dispatch and is not expected
to be affected. Rack 3.1 and 3.2 are affected. Rack 2.2 did not
receive the CVE-2026-34835 change and returns the raw value from
every host method.

advisory.title: Multipart parser retains parsed data in its scan buffer, allowing denial of service via memory exhaustion.
advisory.description:
Rack::Multipart::Parser reads the request body in chunks of
rack.multipart.buffer_size (1 MiB by default) into an internal
scan buffer. Parsed bytes are only discarded from that buffer
when a chunk ends inside a part body. A request whose parts are
sized so that every chunk ends inside, or immediately after, a
part's headers is never compacted, so the buffer grows to the
size of the request.

This results in a denial of service condition through memory
exhaustion for applications that parse multipart requests.

## Impact

Any application that parses multipart requests with Rack is affected
in its default configuration. An unauthenticated attacker can cause
a single request to hold memory proportional to its size for the
duration of parsing, exhausting worker memory. The attack requires
only a well-formed multipart body.

advisory.title: Multipart boundary guard skips a leading empty or quoted `boundary` parameter, allowing parser differentials and WAF bypass
advisory.description:
The guard added for CVE-2026-26961 (GHSA-vgpv-f759-9wx3), which
rejects multipart requests with more than one boundary parameter,
only inspects the part of the Content-Type header after the boundary
it extracts. A Content-Type whose first boundary parameter is empty
or begins with a quote, semicolon, or comma is skipped by the
extraction pattern, so a second boundary parameter is accepted
silently and Rack parses the body with a boundary that a conforming
parser would not derive from the header.

## Impact

As with CVE-2026-26961, an attacker can craft a multipart request that
a web application firewall or other inspecting proxy in front of a
Rack application interprets differently from Rack, so form fields
and file uploads reach the application without inspection. Rack
itself grants no capability beyond that of a well-formed request with
the same body. All supported versions, including 2.2, are affected.

advisory.title: Rack::Static `header_rules` bypass via unnormalized dot segments in the request path
advisory.description:
Rack::Static normalizes the request path with Utils.clean_path_info
when deciding which file to serve, but matches header_rules against
a path that is only URL-decoded. A request containing dot segments,
raw or percent-encoded, is served the normalized target file while
the header rules for that file's location are not applied.

This allows an attacker to receive a protected static file without
the security headers configured for it.

## Impact

Applications that use Rack::Static header_rules to attach
security-relevant headers to particular paths or file types are
affected. An unauthenticated attacker who knows the path of a
protected file can request it through a dot segment path and
receive it without those headers, for example without
Content-Disposition: attachment or a restrictive Content-Security-Policy
that prevents uploaded HTML from rendering inline. The file itself
is served unchanged. Applications that do not use path-specific
header_rules are not affected.

advisory.title: Possible XSS vulnerability with certain configurations of rails-html-sanitizer
advisory.description:
## Summary

There is a possible cross-site scripting vulnerability in
rails-html-sanitizer when the sanitizer is configured to allow an
SVG reference element such as <use>.
See related GHSA-9wjq-cp2p-hrgf in Loofah, whose SVG local-reference
logic rails-html-sanitizer mirrors.

## Impact

`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` restricts SVG reference elements in the
`SVG_ALLOW_LOCAL_HREF` collection to local, same-document references,
but that restriction covered only the `xlink:href` attribute. Browsers
also accept a plain `href` attribute per the SVG 2 spec, and it was
not restricted, so those elements could reference arbitrary external
documents. SVG `<use>` can load and render external SVG content by
reference, and if the referenced document is same-origin and contains
scripts, it could execute in the context of the sanitized document.
`<feImage>` can load external images, which can be used for tracking.

Applications are impacted only when the allowed tags are overridden
to include one of these SVG reference elements, for example `<use>`
or `<feImage>`. The default allowed tags do not include these SVG
elements, so applications using the default configuration are not affected.

## Credit

Found by maintainer Mike Dalessio during a security audit.

advisory.title: Possible regular expression denial of service with certain configurations of rails-html-sanitizer
advisory.description:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` restricts the `href` and `xlink:href` attributes
of SVG reference elements to local references. That check matched the
attribute value against `/^\s*[^#\s].*/m`. In Ruby `^` anchors to every line
start and `\s` matches newlines, so an all-whitespace value made the engine
rescan the value from each of its line starts, taking time quadratic in its
length.

- Versions affected: `>= 1.0.3, < 1.7.2`
- Not affected: `< 1.0.3`
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

CRuby 3.1 and earlier, and JRuby, are affected. CRuby 3.2 added linear-time
regexp matching, which makes the pattern linear. JRuby's regexp engine does
not.

## Impact

An attacker who supplies HTML to be sanitized can consume CPU out of
proportion to the input size, by sending an SVG reference element whose `href`
or `xlink:href` is a long run of whitespace.

Applications are affected only when the allowed tags are overridden to include
an SVG reference element such as `use`, along with `href` or `xlink:href` in
the allowed attributes. The default allowed tags include no SVG elements, so
the default configuration is not affected. Applications that use Loofah
directly are exposed through its own copy of the check, fixed in Loofah
2.25.3.

## Workarounds

On CRuby, run 3.2 or later, which matches the pattern in linear time.
Alternatively, remove the SVG reference elements from the overridden allowed
tags.

## References

- [GHSA-mf2j-8f84-cc9q: the same flaw in
  Loofah](https://github.com/flavorjones/loofah/security/advisories/GHSA-mf2j-8f84-cc9q)
- [CWE-1333: Inefficient Regular Expression
  Complexity](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/1333.html)
- [Ruby 3.2.0 release
  notes](https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2022/12/25/ruby-3-2-0-released/)

## Credit

Reported by scyoon through the Rails HackerOne program.

advisory.title: Possible XSS via shared scrubber state in concurrent rails-html-sanitizer calls
advisory.description:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::SafeListSanitizer` (both the HTML4 and HTML5 variants) shares
one `Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` across every `sanitize` call on the same
instance, assigning its `tags` and `attributes` on each call without
synchronization. Two concurrent `sanitize` calls with different `tags:` or
`attributes:` options can interleave, so one call is scrubbed with the other
call's allowlist.

- Versions affected: `< 1.7.2`
- Not affected: none
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

## Impact

Action View memoizes a single `SafeListSanitizer` per helper module and uses
it for every `sanitize` call in the process, so in a multi-threaded server
(for example Puma) all requests share the same `PermitScrubber`. If any code
path calls `sanitize` with a more permissive allowlist, an attacker who can
trigger that path concurrently with another request can cause the other
request to be sanitized with the permissive allowlist. If the permissive
allowlist admits `script` or an event-handler attribute, the strict call emits
it unchanged, which is a cross-site scripting vector when the strict output is
stored or rendered to other users.

Applications are affected only if they run more than one thread per process
and some `sanitize` call passes `tags:` or `attributes:` options that differ
from another call's, including a call that passes no options and so uses the
defaults. Applications that use a single configuration everywhere, pass their
own `scrubber:`, or run single-threaded are not affected.

## Workarounds

Use the same allowlist for every `sanitize` call, or pass a `scrubber:` built
per call (`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber.new` with `tags=` and `attributes=`
set) instead of `tags:` and `attributes:` options.

## References

- [CWE-362: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper
  Synchronization ('Race
  Condition')](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/362.html)
- [CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation
  ('Cross-site Scripting')](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/79.html)
- [rails/rails-html-sanitizer#228](https://github.com/rails/rails-html-sanitizer/issues/228)

## Credit

Reported by hiumee via HackerOne.

advisory.title: path traversal vulnerability in pre-3.4.0 rubyzip gem
advisory.description:
rubyzip versions before 3.4.0 contain a path traversal vulnerability
in Zip::Entry#extract that fails to properly validate extraction
paths using prefix comparison without trailing separators. Attackers
can craft archive entries with names like ../upload_backup/owned.sh
to write files outside the intended extraction directory into
sibling paths sharing the destination prefix.

advisory.title: Use-After-Free When Redefining SQLite Functions with Different Arity
advisory.description:
## Summary

Using Database#create_function or Database#define_function to define
the same function name more than once with different numbers of
arguments ("arity") or text encodings will result in a invalid memory
read and a segmentation fault.

## Severity

The sqlite3-ruby repo maintainers assess this as Low severity. It is
reliably triggered after GC when code is structured in a particular way.
There is no known general exploit that could be used as a denial
of service attack.

advisory.title: Use-After-Free in SQLite Aggregate Function Callbacks
advisory.description:
## Summary

Using Database#create_aggregate, #create_aggregate_handler, or
Database#define_aggregator to define an aggregate function, and
then using an open statement calling that function after the database
has been explicitly closed will result in an invalid memory read
and a segmentation fault.

## Severity

The sqlite3-ruby repo maintainers assess this as Low severity. It is
reliably triggered after GC when code is structured in a particular way.
There is no known general exploit that could be used as a denial
of service attack.

advisory.title: Possible SQL query truncation when a string is 4 GiB or larger
advisory.description:
sqlite3-ruby cast Ruby string lengths (long) to int before passing
them to SQLite. On 64-bit platforms, a string of 4 GiB (2^32 bytes)
or larger had its length wrap, so SQLite saw only the first length
mod 2^32 bytes. An attacker who controls the length of a SQL string
could truncate the query, for example dropping a trailing WHERE
clause. The affected paths are:

* the SQL passed to Database#prepare, #execute, and related methods
* String and Blob values passed to Statement#bind_param and related methods
* String and Blob values returned from SQL functions and aggregates
  defined in Ruby (Database#create_function, #create_aggregate, and
  related methods)

## AFTER PATCH

sqlite3 v2.10.2 raises RangeError when any of these strings is
longer than INT_MAX bytes.

## Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Luke Jahnke from elttam.

advisory.title: Use-After-Free in SQLite Aggregate Arguments in Heap-Allocated Argument Array
advisory.description:
## Summary

Using Database#create_aggregate, #create_aggregate_handler, or
Database#define_aggregator to define an aggregate function that takes
two or more arguments, and then evaluating it over TEXT or BLOB column
values, can free the Ruby objects holding those arguments while a
later argument is still being converted, during ordinary garbage
collection. The aggregate's step method then receives an incorrect
object, or the process crashes with a segmentation fault.

## Credits

Reported by Jeremy Daer (@jeremy).

advisory.title: Use-After-Free When Redefining SQLite Functions with Different Arity
advisory.description:
## Summary

Using Database#create_function or Database#define_function to define
the same function name more than once with different numbers of
arguments ("arity") or text encodings will result in a invalid memory
read and a segmentation fault.

## Severity

The sqlite3-ruby repo maintainers assess this as Low severity. It is
reliably triggered after GC when code is structured in a particular way.
There is no known general exploit that could be used as a denial
of service attack.

advisory.title: Use-After-Free in SQLite Aggregate Function Callbacks
advisory.description:
## Summary

Using Database#create_aggregate, #create_aggregate_handler, or
Database#define_aggregator to define an aggregate function, and
then using an open statement calling that function after the database
has been explicitly closed will result in an invalid memory read
and a segmentation fault.

## Severity

The sqlite3-ruby repo maintainers assess this as Low severity. It is
reliably triggered after GC when code is structured in a particular way.
There is no known general exploit that could be used as a denial
of service attack.

advisory.title: Possible SQL query truncation when a string is 4 GiB or larger
advisory.description:
sqlite3-ruby cast Ruby string lengths (long) to int before passing
them to SQLite. On 64-bit platforms, a string of 4 GiB (2^32 bytes)
or larger had its length wrap, so SQLite saw only the first length
mod 2^32 bytes. An attacker who controls the length of a SQL string
could truncate the query, for example dropping a trailing WHERE
clause. The affected paths are:

* the SQL passed to Database#prepare, #execute, and related methods
* String and Blob values passed to Statement#bind_param and related methods
* String and Blob values returned from SQL functions and aggregates
  defined in Ruby (Database#create_function, #create_aggregate, and
  related methods)

## AFTER PATCH

sqlite3 v2.10.2 raises RangeError when any of these strings is
longer than INT_MAX bytes.

## Credit

This issue was responsibly reported by Luke Jahnke from elttam.

advisory.title: Use-After-Free in SQLite Aggregate Arguments in Heap-Allocated Argument Array
advisory.description:
## Summary

Using Database#create_aggregate, #create_aggregate_handler, or
Database#define_aggregator to define an aggregate function that takes
two or more arguments, and then evaluating it over TEXT or BLOB column
values, can free the Ruby objects holding those arguments while a
later argument is still being converted, during ordinary garbage
collection. The aggregate's step method then receives an incorrect
object, or the process crashes with a segmentation fault.

## Credits

Reported by Jeremy Daer (@jeremy).

advisory.title: Denial of service via malformed Host header
advisory.description:
## Impact

If this library is used to implement a WebSocket server on top of a
TCP server, by using the WebSocket::Driver.server() method, then a
client can cause the server to crash by sending a Host header that
is not a valid host[:port] string. When this happens, a URI::InvalidURIError
exception is raised which is not caught, and this can cause the server
process to crash if the application does not catch the error from
 the parse() method itself.

## Acknowledgements

This issue was discovered and reported by Pranjali Thakur,
DepthFirst Security Research Team.
